title: Know when to ask the big model
dek: A cheap model that hands only its unsure cases to a frontier one nearly matched it at a quarter of the cost. Also: agents that stop early and call it done, a spec checked against live traffic, and how SEED keeps a player-built world fast.

theme.mood: a Saturday about knowing what you do not know

tldr.text: Hightouch let a cheap model grade its data and send only the scores it was unsure about to Opus: **98.8% accuracy at about a quarter of the cost** on the easy test, 1.8 times cheaper on the hard one.
On a new benchmark of 5 to 15 linked coding steps, the best agent finished only 18.5% of tasks, and in about half the failed steps the agent claimed it was done.
SEED's Unity team found that animated level-of-detail fades had quietly switched off the fast drawing path on PC; on phones, memory was the limit.
Epic said at Unreal Fest Tokyo that Unreal Engine 5.9 previews the week after with the web as a target, and the first Unreal 6 preview lands in the second half of 2027.
Beholder: Conductor sold 81,088 copies in 14 days, 15 months after launch, about as many as at launch.

blocks.title: A cheap grader that hands its unsure cases to Opus
blocks.gist: Hightouch had a fast, cheap AI model check its customer data and pass only the cases it was unsure about to an expensive one. The mix was nearly as accurate as the expensive model alone, for about a quarter of the cost.
blocks.background: Hightouch merges records that belong to the same person into one profile. The failure it fears most is a profile that wrongly mixes two different people.
blocks.takeaway: A cheap model is worth routing only if its confidence means something. Jev's mistakes sat in the middle of its scale, so sending that middle band to Opus caught them; a more accurate but overconfident model made a worse partner.
body: In a November 4 post, Hightouch engineers Albert Jin, Neil Desai and Delaney Mackenzie tested AI judges on 1,000 synthetic profiles, half of them wrongly merged. Opus 5.5 alone was 99.0% accurate at $3.86 per 1,000 checks and 2.2 seconds each. A small "decision model" called Jev was 95.7% accurate at $0.05 and 0.15 seconds.

Then they combined them. Jev scores every profile from 0 to 1; anything in an escalation band between 30% and 90% goes to Opus for a second opinion. That sent 22% of profiles to Opus and reached **98.8% accuracy at $0.88 per 1,000**, about 4.4 times cheaper than Opus alone.

The headline holds only on the easy test. On a harder set full of typos and look-alike people (twins, father and son), Opus alone scored 95.1% at $5.39 and the mix 95.3% at $2.94: still as good, but only 1.8 times cheaper.

The surprise was which cheap model worked. GPT-6 Luna beat Jev alone on the easy test, but many of its mistakes came with 90 to 100% confidence, so no band could catch them. The data is synthetic and the authors say their costs will not carry over exactly.

stat.label: of checks sent to Opus in the best mix, for 98.8% accuracy (Opus alone: 99.0%)

image.alt: Bar chart of Jev's mistakes by confidence bucket on the easy test: none below 20%, peaking at 8 and 9 mistakes in the 40 to 60% buckets, with far fewer Opus mistakes on the same profiles.

terms.def: A small model built to answer one narrow question fast and return a confidence score instead of a written explanation.
The range of confidence scores, such as 30% to 90%, that gets passed to a stronger model for a second look.
Saying it is very sure on answers that turn out to be wrong, so its confidence cannot be used to spot mistakes.

deep: Harder test: Jev alone 89.1% ($0.06), Luna alone 88.8% ($0.12), hybrid Luna 91.6% ($1.15), hybrid Jev 95.3% ($2.94, 1.56 s), Opus alone 95.1% ($5.39, 2.6 s). The authors do not give the size of the harder set.

Prompting: listing common error types in the prompt helped every model most. Adding context about the data sources added at most about one point for frontier models and nothing for the decision models.
blocks.why: Any pipeline that uses a model to grade, review or triage can copy this: score cheaply, escalate the uncertain middle. But first plot where the cheap model's mistakes fall, because the trick only works when they sit in the middle.
blocks.forYou: The same split fits the routines' triage and any review step in the SaaS backends: a cheap pass with a confidence score, Opus only for the middle band. Plot the cheap model's mistakes by confidence on a labelled sample before trusting it.

sources.label: Hightouch: LLM judges for identity resolution

blocks.title: SEED tested on its players' biggest city and found two different bottlenecks
blocks.gist: The makers of SEED, an online world players build themselves, profiled the game on a copy of the busiest real island. On PC a smooth-looking fade between detail levels had switched off the fast drawing path; on phones, memory ran out first.
blocks.background: SEED is Klang Games' persistent sandbox in early access, built in Unity: players run settlements on a distant planet while a server runs the simulation.
blocks.plain: Test on the worst real world your players have built, not a tidy test level, and expect each platform to break for a different reason.
body: Klang restores its server's disaster-recovery snapshots on a developer machine and uses them as test scenes. The busiest island holds **172 buildings, about 12,500 voxels and about 190,000 modules**, since each voxel expands into roughly 15 pieces.

On PC the game was limited by the CPU thread that sends draw calls. Most props use LOD groups, and their animated cross-fade kept them off Unity's GPU Resident Drawer, which batches copies of the same mesh, so they were drawn one by one. Turning the animation off and setting transitions by hand brought instancing back.

On phones the limit was memory. Snapshot diffs found a texture stored three times through a broken reference, a material duplicated by asset dependencies and oversized collections. Trees with every LOD loaded cost megabytes each, so mobile now loads simpler trees and uses Mesh LOD, which keeps all levels in one mesh.

image.alt: A dusk view over a dense player-built town in SEED: lit apartment blocks, rooftop gardens, neon signs and trees.

terms.def: Cube-shaped building blocks on a grid, like 3D pixels.
Requests the CPU sends to the graphics card to draw something; too many and the CPU becomes the bottleneck.
Level of detail: simpler versions of a model swapped in when it is far from the camera.
Blending smoothly between two detail levels instead of switching at once.
Drawing many copies of the same mesh in one request to the graphics card.
A Unity 6.2 feature that stores all detail levels inside a single mesh instead of separate objects.

deep: Stack: Unity 6.3 with URP defaults, BatchRendererGroup with the C# Job System and Burst for the building modules, Shader Graph. Surface color, metalness and smoothness are baked into vertices rather than textures. Interiors generate only when a player looks inside.

Tools: Unity Profiler and Frame Debugger on PC to see the render thread and which objects went through the SRP Batcher (one draw per object) instead of the GPU Resident Drawer (instanced batches); Memory Profiler snapshot diffs on mobile; per-platform Addressables builds. The article gives no frame times or memory totals.
blocks.why: Synthetic test levels hide the problems real players create. Profiling a copy of the worst live world, platform by platform, is an engine-agnostic habit any team with saves or server backups can adopt.
blocks.forYou: For the action RPG, keep a library of the heaviest real save files and profile them per platform; in Unreal, check whether dithered LOD transitions or Nanite fallbacks are breaking batching the same way.

sources.label: Unity: How SEED renders a world players never stop building

blocks.title: Saving a game where time rewinds but the hero remembers
blocks.gist: In Sovereign Tower a demon can rewind time, but the ruler remembers everything. Its makers found ordinary save files could not handle that, and rebuilt saving in small separate pieces.
blocks.plain: When some state rewinds and some does not, save them apart, in many small pieces, and test the joins hard.
body: Wild Wits Games' narrative management RPG, out on Steam for Windows and Linux, needs two saves per played cycle, morning and afternoon, and each must reflect every earlier cycle. With hundreds of story variables and quests and over a hundred characters, lead programmer Paul Mozet called it a "perfect bug factory".

Simple whole-state saves broke because the ruler keeps what they learned across rewinds. The team split saved data into as many pieces as possible and tested heavily; some bugs still shipped and are being patched. They also cut story variants to keep word count and translation costs down.

image.alt: Sovereign Tower screenshot: a smiling knight in a fur cloak between a quest card for The Vampire of Clovermont and a stat wheel, with a Cycle 3 counter top left.

terms.def: One in-game day in Sovereign Tower, the unit the rewind jumps back across.

deep: Built in Godot. The art director updates portraits directly in Godot scenes; the team mixes AnimationPlayers and Tweens, and says UI animation got much easier once Godot 4.7 added transform offsets, which move controls without fighting layout containers.
blocks.why: Any game with time travel, roguelike carry-over or branching story has state that survives a reset and state that does not. Deciding that split before writing the save format saves months of bugs.
blocks.forYou: Worth a look before the action RPG's save format hardens: separate what persists across deaths or reloads from what resets.

blocks.title: How a 2001 RPG was remastered with no source code
blocks.gist: SNEG re-released the 2001 RPG Pool of Radiance: Ruins of Myth Drannor with 4K, controller and Steam Deck support, working only from the old retail discs. The tricks suit any game whose code is lost.
blocks.intro: The re-release came out on Steam and GOG on November 6. Co-founder Artem Shchuiko told 80 Level the team had no source, tools or documentation.

steps.title: Start from the retail discs
steps.text: Use the international retail editions and reverse-engineer just enough to change the original engine from inside the old build.

steps.title: Build a data bridge
steps.text: Write an internal API that exposes the game data the new interface needs. Shchuiko called this the hardest part, since much of it was buried in the original code.

steps.title: Layer a new interface
steps.text: Draw the new action bar, tooltips and menus with Dear ImGui, chosen because it let the team iterate fastest. New UI art was drawn at twice the old resolution.

steps.title: Sharpen, keep the rules
steps.text: Use AMD FSR 1.0 to sharpen without touching original art, rebuild the font with missing letters, change core systems only for clear bugs, and keep an optional Legacy mode.

image.alt: Isometric combat in a dungeon: a party fights a drow warrior inside a blue spell circle, with a combat log top left, a new action bar along the bottom and controller button prompts.

terms.def: A small open-source library for drawing interface panels in code, popular for game tools and debug menus.
AMD FidelityFX Super Resolution, a free upscaling and sharpening filter that runs on most graphics cards.

blocks.why: Remasters, ports and mods of lost-source games follow this recipe: expose data first, then draw a modern interface over the old engine.
blocks.forYou: The data-bridge-then-new-UI order also suits wrapping a legacy plugin's internals before a UI rewrite.

blocks.gist: At Unreal Fest Tokyo, Epic said Unreal Engine 5.9 would preview the following week with the web as a target, and that the first Unreal 6 preview is planned for the second half of 2027.
blocks.background: Epic has said Unreal 6 will move gameplay code to its Verse language and drop Blueprints and the C++ gameplay framework.
blocks.intro: The dates Epic gave, from its Japanese press release for the November 3 and 4 event.

Epic tests the move from Blueprints to Verse in Fortnite first, then shares lessons and migration tools.
First Unreal 6 preview, with Unreal and Fortnite's editor merged into one engine.

terms.def: Epic's programming language for gameplay, first used in Fortnite's creator tools.
Model Context Protocol, an open standard that lets AI assistants call tools and apps.

blocks.why: A web export in 5.9 would put Unreal back in the browser, and a 2027 preview date sets how long plugin and project code stays on today's framework.
blocks.forYou: Watch the 5.9 preview notes for the web target's limits for browser builds, and plan Fab plugin support on UE5 through at least 2027; the Fortnite migration tools will be the first hint of how C++ plugins port.

blocks.title: A 15-month-old game sold as much in two weeks as at launch
blocks.gist: Beholder: Conductor matched its launch sales more than a year later by stacking a discount, a Steam front-page deal, a Steam festival feature and a paid creator campaign at once.
body: GameDiscoverCo's October roundup says most buyers came from recent wishlists, and the wishlist pool kept growing during the sale. The newsletter credits a discount, a Daily Deal, a Steam Train Fest feature and a paid creator campaign.

terms.def: A one-day discount Steam features on its front page.
Steam's save-for-later list; wishlisters get an email when a game goes on sale.

blocks.why: A game's launch is not its only sales spike. Stacking store features with fresh marketing can bring a second launch, fed by new wishlists.
blocks.forYou: For back-catalogue Fab and Steam products, plan one stacked moment (discount, feature, creator push) instead of spreading small sales.

blocks.title: Win back lapsed players, and prove the ads did it
blocks.gist: The studio behind Supremacy 1914 shows ads to former players and compares their spending against a group that sees none. Its first test showed no effect until it split players by how much they used to spend.
blocks.background: Twin Harbour Interactive is a Stillfront studio making mobile strategy games; it began re-engagement about 18 months ago as the cost of new installs rose.
blocks.intro: Faisal Nimri, senior growth marketing manager, described the method to PocketGamer.biz ahead of a talk in Jordan.

steps.title: Hold some players back
steps.text: Show ads to 80% of an audience and none to 20%. The revenue difference between the two groups is the real effect. Small studios can use 50/50, which reaches a clear answer in about two weeks instead of four.

steps.title: Split before you test
steps.text: The first broad test showed no uplift. Separate non-payers from payers, and split payers into high, mid and low spenders.

steps.title: Race the channels
steps.text: Give two ad channels 40% of a segment each, keep 20% as control, and after three to four weeks pit the winner against a new challenger.

steps.title: Give a new reason
steps.text: Time pushes to a big update or a seasonal peak, use new creative instead of install ads, and run an extra week rather than stop before the result is clear. Start with 5 to 10% of the install budget.

terms.def: A group of players who see no ads, so you can measure what would have happened anyway.
Crediting an install or purchase to the ad a player saw last, whether or not the ad caused it.

deep: Twin Harbour uses AppsFlyer's incrementality product because its attribution provider already had the audiences and integrations. Seasonal peaks it targets: Christmas in the US and Europe, Ramadan and Eid in the Middle East and North Africa.
blocks.why: Retargeting looks great on attribution dashboards because many players would have come back anyway. A held-out group is the cheapest honest measure.
blocks.forYou: Before paying to re-engage players of the mobile titles, hold back a 50/50 control and tie the push to an update.

sources.label: PocketGamer.biz: How Twin Harbour wins back lapsed players

blocks.title: Agents that keep building on their own code mostly fail
blocks.gist: A new benchmark asks coding agents to extend their own code through 5 to 15 linked steps. The best model finished 18.5% of tasks, and in about half of failed steps the agent said it was done.
blocks.intro: Share of 69 tasks fully solved (every step passing), average of four runs each.
blocks.note: 38 of the 69 tasks were solved by no model. A step after a passed step passed 70.2% of the time; after a failed one, 14.1%. In 52% of failed steps the agent reported success and named no failing check. MiMo 2.6 Pro (2.9%) is left off the chart.

terms.def: A fixed set of tasks used to compare systems on equal terms.

deep: Multi-step SWE, from Klavis AI (Xiangkai Zeng, Zheng Liu, Zihao Lin; arXiv, November 4): four task families in nine languages. Best model by family: optimization 34.7%, migration 19.2%, feature work 12.5%, version upgrades 8.8%. Checks rebuild the program from source, hide expected outputs, generate inputs at grading time and run the agent as a user who cannot write the score file.
blocks.why: Errors compound: one bad step makes the next far likelier to fail, and agents often say they are done anyway. Long agent runs need a real check after every step, not a final one.
blocks.forYou: Split long routines into steps with their own pass or fail check, and stop the chain on the first failure instead of letting the agent continue on a broken base.

blocks.title: Turn agent rules into scripts that fail
blocks.gist: A developer argues that rules written in an agent's instruction file are suggestions it can bend, while a script that exits with an error is not. His own rule check failed 9 of 10 replies in one session.
blocks.plain: If a rule matters, write it as a check that runs and fails, not as a sentence the agent may skip.
body: Daniel Nwaneri's post on DEV says files like CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md are recommendations. He moves rules into scripts the agent must run, such as lint, format and test scripts or make targets, and into hooks and CI gates that block work when a rule is broken.

His example: a 20-word sentence limit written as a script flagged 9 of 10 of his agent's replies in one session, so he wired it into a hook. Commenters add two refinements: keep the checker where the agent cannot edit it, and plant one known violation to prove the check can fail.
points: Rules in prose drift in long sessions; exit codes do not.
Run the check from a hook, a make target and CI.
Keep the checker outside the agent's write access.
Seed one deliberate failure to test the test.

terms.def: A Markdown file of project instructions that Claude Code reads at the start of a session.
Commands a coding agent's harness runs automatically before or after a tool call.
Continuous integration: automatic checks that run on every push or pull request.

blocks.why: Today's benchmark shows agents declaring success without proof. A rule that runs as code gives them, and you, a signal they cannot argue with.
blocks.forYou: Go through the CLAUDE.md files and move every rule that can be checked mechanically (dash ban, colour ids, no raw HTML) into a hook script; the Radar validator already proves the pattern.

sources.label: DEV: Don't write Markdown files for your coding agent. Write scripts.

blocks.title: Datadog checks a formal spec against live production traffic
blocks.gist: Datadog turned the precise written model of how its event routing should behave into a monitor that watches the real system. It caught a year-old bug that ordinary tests never hit, at about 2% extra CPU.
blocks.background: TLA+ is a language for describing what a system is allowed to do, step by step, so the design can be checked before or after it is built.
blocks.intro: FETCh, the Formal Execution Trace Checker, compiles each allowed step in a TLA+ spec into a small Rust check that reads the system's own logs.

nodes.label: Spec
nodes.note: TLA+ lists each allowed action and its preconditions.

nodes.label: Monitor
nodes.note: Each action becomes a Rust function that checks and applies it.

nodes.label: Live logs
nodes.note: A sidecar on 1,300+ pods feeds real events in.

nodes.label: Divergence
nodes.note: A failed precondition means code and spec disagree.

nodes.label: Fix
nodes.note: Found before customers saw a symptom.

blocks.caption: The bug: special cases added a year earlier skipped a duplicate check, leaving conflicting placements in under 0.01% of records. Two were enough to crash recovery after a data loss.

terms.def: An exact, checkable description of what a system may and may not do.
A specification language by Leslie Lamport for modelling concurrent and distributed systems.
A helper process that runs next to a service and reads its output without changing it.
Something that must be true before an action is allowed to happen.

deep: Written by Nicolas Couvrat for Husky, Datadog's event store, which handles millions of events a second. Overhead across more than 1,300 routing pods: about 2% CPU at p90 and under 0.2% memory. Batch mode checked several days of data (several million placements) in about an hour on one CPU.
Limits the post lists: only a subset of TLA+ is supported, preconditions are checked against current state only, and instrumenting a distributed system takes real engineering time.
blocks.why: Specs usually drift from code the day after they are written. Checking the spec against production keeps it honest and finds the rare cases tests never generate.
blocks.forYou: The same idea scales down: write the invariants of a Supabase-backed workflow (no double booking, one owner per record) as checks over production logs or rows, and run them nightly.

blocks.title: Ghostty's terminal engine is now a stable library
blocks.gist: Mitchell Hashimoto released version 1.0 of libghostty, the core of his Ghostty terminal, as a library any app can embed, from IDEs to web pages.
blocks.name: libghostty 1.0
blocks.what: The terminal core of Ghostty as a portable C library with a stable interface, MIT licensed.
body: Apps that show a terminal, such as editors, agent dashboards and dev tools, can embed it instead of writing their own emulator. Hashimoto says JetBrains IDE terminals already use it, along with Vercel's Turborepo and OrbStack.
A complete build for the web is under 1 MB, and a working terminal takes about 1,500 lines of C. Bindings exist for Rust, Go, JavaScript, Swift, Python and Dart.

facts.v: Linux, macOS, iOS, Windows, Android, FreeBSD, WebAssembly
10,000 active terminals on a 4-core, 8 GB server

terms.def: The binary interface between compiled programs; a stable one means apps keep working when the library updates.
A compact code format that runs in browsers at near-native speed.

deep: The stable ABI uses opaque handles and enum-keyed getters and setters, so new options need no new symbols; newer headers against older libraries return GHOSTTY_UNSUPPORTED instead of crashing. CI checks the ABI with libabigail. Kitty graphics, search, selection and input encoding can be compiled out.
blocks.why: A fast, maintained terminal engine with a stable interface lowers the cost of building tools that show agent or build output live, in native apps or the browser.
blocks.forYou: A candidate for any browser or desktop tool that streams agent sessions; the WebAssembly build could replace xterm.js where fidelity matters.

blocks.title: Claude Code 2.1.319: deny instead of waiting, and three bypass fixes
blocks.gist: The latest Claude Code adds a setting that refuses any action needing approval instead of waiting for a person, which suits unattended runs, and closes three ways around its permission checks.
blocks.intro: The new setting, in settings.json. A call that would stop at a permission prompt is denied and the turn carries on, in terminal sessions, subagents and teammates.
explain: Fixed: a crafted environment prefix that hid part of a Bash command from permission checks, a sed command skipping the check in accept-edits and auto mode, and a sandbox escape when creating a worktree. Update now.

Also changed: self-paced /loop now ends when a turn finishes without rescheduling (CLAUDE_CODE_LOOP_KEEPALIVE=1 keeps the old behavior), and claude -p exits 1 instead of 0 when auto mode refused actions.

terms.def: A Claude Code mode where a safety check, not a person, approves most actions.
A second working folder for the same git repository, used to run agents in parallel.

deep: MCP tool calls that a server runs as tasks now go to the background at once, and Claude is told the result when they finish (CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASK_BACKGROUND waits instead). New /claude-api latency-optimize finds where API code makes people wait. /tasks gains an Earlier in this session row to reopen finished subagents. The Bash tool now asks before running which with unusual flags.
blocks.why: Unattended agent runs used to stall on a prompt nobody would answer. Denying and continuing, plus a non-zero exit code, lets scripts notice and report instead of hanging.
blocks.forYou: Set denyInsteadOfPrompting in the routines' settings and check any self-paced /loop that relied on the fallback wakeup.

groups.note: Agents that say they are done, rules that run as code, a spec watching production, and the tools around them.

learn.question: What does it mean for a model to be well calibrated?
learn.answer: A model is well calibrated when its confidence matches how often it is right: of all the answers it gives at 70% confidence, about 70% turn out correct. Then its confidence tells you which answers to double-check.
learn.analogy: A weather forecaster who says "70% chance of rain" is calibrated if it rains on about seven of every ten such days.
body: Accuracy and calibration are different things. A model can be right more often overall and still be badly calibrated, if it is just as sure of its wrong answers as of its right ones.

Calibration is what makes routing possible. In today's lead story, the cheap model's mistakes clustered around 50% confidence, so sending only its middle scores to a stronger model caught most of them. The other cheap model was more accurate but often wrong at 90 to 100% confidence, and no band could catch those.

To check a model yourself, run it on a few hundred labelled examples, group its answers by confidence and count how many in each group were right. The more those counts match the confidence, the more you can trust the score.

nodes.label: Score
nodes.note: The model gives each answer a confidence, like 0.7.

nodes.label: Group
nodes.note: Put answers with similar confidence together.

nodes.label: Count
nodes.note: Check how many in each group were right.

diagram.caption: Calibrated scores tell you where the mistakes are, which is what lets a cheap model hand off only its doubtful cases.

terms.def: The probability a model attaches to its own answer.
Sending each request to a different model depending on how hard or uncertain it looks.

tryThis.title: Profile your game on the heaviest real save, not a test level
tryThis.gist: You find the slowdowns real players will hit, using the method SEED's team used to find a batching path that was quietly turned off and assets loaded twice.
tryThis.needs: A game with save files, player levels or server backups, and your engine's CPU and memory profilers.

steps.title: Pick the worst real state
steps.text: Take the biggest save, player-made level or server backup you have and load it as a test scene, the way Klang restores its disaster-recovery snapshots.

steps.title: Find the limit
steps.text: Run the CPU profiler and see whether the main or render thread is the limit. If it is the render thread, open the frame debugger and look for objects drawn one at a time that should be batched or instanced.

steps.title: Switch off one nicety
steps.text: Turn off animated LOD fades (in Unity, the LOD Group's cross-fade animation) and measure again. SEED got instancing back this way.

steps.title: Diff memory on mobile
steps.text: Take a memory snapshot after loading, play a minute, take another, and compare them. Look for the same texture or material loaded more than once.

tryThis.check: Draw calls or render-thread time fall after the change, or the snapshot diff names an asset loaded twice that you can fix.

terms.def: A tool that steps through every draw call in one frame and shows how each object was drawn.
A record of everything loaded in memory at one moment, which can be compared with another.

tryThis.forYou: Load the heaviest action RPG test save in Unreal Insights, and check whether dithered LOD transitions are breaking instanced draws; for the three.js games, the same idea applies with the browser's performance panel.

sources.label: Unity: How SEED renders a world players never stop building

sparks.title: World Strike: toy tanks that flatten real city blocks, for everyone
sparks.signal: 167 points and 119 comments on Hacker News on November 6; the creator reported about 7,500 buildings destroyed since posting.
sparks.hook: Pick any city, drive a tank down its real streets and knock buildings down. The rubble stays for every later player in that spot.
sparks.borrow: Building outlines from OpenStreetMap, extruded to boxes, make any city a level. The creator's launch fixes are a checklist: collision tested too many buildings, the server dropped inputs when behind, and a 5-minute respawn became 30 seconds.

image.alt: Top-down view of an Amsterdam canal street with brick buildings on one side and a block knocked flat into rubble, a small yellow tank on the road, and the World Strike title card.
image.credit: World Strike, map data OpenStreetMap contributors

sparks.forYou: A weekend three.js prototype for the browser games: OSM footprints plus shared persistent destruction is a strong hook.

sparks.title: LDraw Mecha: agents read a Lego model and animate its moving parts
sparks.signal: Small and early: 25 points on Show HN and 13 GitHub stars on November 6, a follow-up to the same author's agent-built Lego CAD tool.
sparks.hook: Agents read a Lego model's source file, work out which parts are mechanisms, plan how they move, then write Blender Python to rig and animate them, such as a Technic crane's arm.
sparks.borrow: Plan on the model's structure, not on pixels, then emit engine scripts. The same plan-then-script split could rig or animate assets in any engine. The README calls it a very preliminary release.

image.alt: Render of a red, yellow and black Lego Technic crane arm with pneumatic cylinders, rigged and animated in Blender.

sparks.title: Scam With Your Friends: a co-op game where the marks are AI callers
sparks.signal: Over 600,000 sold in October by GameDiscoverCo's estimate, with heavy streamer interest, though player counts are well off their peak.
sparks.hook: Friends run a call center under a raging boss and talk AI-voiced callers into trusting them, in real-time conversations, to hit a daily quota.
sparks.borrow: Talking to AI characters works when the goal is concrete and scored (a trust meter, a quota) and friends can watch each other fail. The fast fade is a warning about replay value.

image.alt: Game screen styled as a desktop: a phone window shows caller Dorothy Mayfield at 65% trust, a form window says the scam earned $250, and a webcam shows the angry boss.

sparks.title: Moon Sweepers: clean the whole Moon, starting with a toothbrush
sparks.signal: Over 700,000 sold in October at about $7.50 by GameDiscoverCo's estimate, after launching on October 23.
sparks.hook: Up to 16 friends sweep lunar dust, sell it and upgrade from a toothbrush to cleaning vehicles. An absurd job turned into an incremental co-op business.
sparks.borrow: A tiny starting tool against a huge task is an instant joke and an upgrade path in one. Large lobbies make slacking off part of the fun.

image.alt: A cartoon astronaut on the Moon pushing a wide broom, with the Earth and a small base behind.

sparks.title: X-87: a whole landscape from 256 bytes of DOS code
sparks.signal: 44 points on Lobsters on November 5; a mainstream developer video about 4 KB coding contests drew 30 more there the same week.
sparks.hook: A 256-byte program for old PCs paints a misty sea and sky by summing oscillators on the floating-point unit, made for the Outline 2026 demoparty.
sparks.borrow: The author sketched it in p5.js years earlier and shrank it later. Prototype a look in a friendly tool, then compress; sums of waves give terrain with no meshes or textures.

image.alt: A grainy blue-white seascape under a stormy sky, rendered by the 256-byte X-87 program.

sparks.title: Kugelblitz: a Mac globe built from open maps
sparks.signal: 246 points and 65 comments on Hacker News on November 6.
sparks.hook: A native Mac globe and atlas by podcaster Tim Pritlove: imagery and topo maps on real terrain, thousands of open maps, a flying mode and a cache shared across a network.
sparks.borrow: Open geodata alone now makes a convincing Earth viewer, the same data World Strike plays on. Commenters say much of it was built with AI help; that is not confirmed by the author.

image.alt: A Mac window showing the Earth from space, Europe and Africa in daylight and the night side dark, with a time slider and map tools.

lab.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
lab.headline: Have the agent write a provable spec first, then review eight promises, not every line
lab.problem: Reviewing agent-written code line by line does not scale, and tests only cover the cases someone thought of.
lab.idea: Proof-driven development: the agent asks the developer short decision questions, writes a formal spec in Verus (a verifier for Rust), and two reviewer agents check it. Then it writes code with proofs, tests cover the pieces outside the proof, and a mutation check plants one bug per clause to show each one bites.
lab.result: One case study, no benchmark: the login logic of a roughly 5,000-line Rust pet store app came down to 8 guarantees about the login function, with 6 trusted pieces (database lookups, password hashing, the clock, token signing) left outside the proof.
lab.useIt: Borrow the shape without Verus: list the promises a feature must keep, name what you trust without proof, and plant one bug per promise to check your tests catch it.

image.alt: PDD Kit pipeline: the team states intent, pdd-plan turns it into decision cards and a formal spec in Verus, pdd-prove checks proofs, tests and gaps, and a pull request ships proved code.

lab.forYou: The mutation check (one planted bug per promise) is cheap to add to the SaaS auth and billing tests even without proofs.

lab.title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
lab.headline: About 30% of a popular agent benchmark's tasks were broken; fixing them moved scores by over 10 points
lab.authors: E. Kelly Buchanan, Crystal Zhou, Scott W. Linderman, et al. (Stanford University, Cornell University)
lab.problem: Agent benchmarks rot: verifiers reject valid solutions, instructions drift from checks, and infrastructure changes break tasks, so scores measure the benchmark's bugs.
lab.idea: Treat the benchmark as software with maintenance: agents gather evidence, an auditor labels each task's defect type, a verifier re-runs the reference solution, repairs come out as reviewable diffs, and a maintainer approves before release.
lab.result: Problems in about 30% of Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks. Fixes raised accuracy by more than 10 points and moved ranks by up to 3 places. A longer time limit closed a 20-point gap between harnesses for one model; timeouts were about two thirds of failed runs for two of the harnesses.
lab.useIt: Before blaming a model or harness for failing your evals, sort the failures into instruction mismatch, drift and environment, and rerun with a longer time limit.

image.alt: Three-part figure: revised tasks by issue type (instruction mismatch 57%, drift 43%, environment 29%); timeouts among failed trials by harness, from 68% for Claude Code to 18% for Gemini CLI; memory and disk issues.

lab.forYou: Run the same sort over the routine's validate failures and any agent eval set before changing models.

lab.title: RIDGE: State-Conditioned Reward Blending for Behavioral Coverage in Deep RL Game Agents
lab.headline: One playtest bot that changes play style mid-game instead of training one bot per style
lab.authors: AL Muqshith Mohammed Shifan, Kevin Christopher Chua, Ali Neshati, et al. (Ontario Tech University)
lab.problem: Automated playtesting usually trains one agent per persona (explorer, survivor, warrior), which multiplies cost, and switching goals mid-episode makes training unstable.
lab.idea: Blend the persona rewards with weights that follow slow-moving game state, such as hunger, and give the critic one value head per persona so learning stays stable while the goal shifts.
lab.result: Preliminary, 3 seeds in the Crafter survival game: the blended agent reached both crafting and combat goals that no single persona reached together, though each specialist still beat it on its own goal (for example wood sword 0.26 against 0.79).
lab.useIt: A pattern to watch for test bots that should cover several behaviours in one run; not yet strong enough to replace specialists.
lab.forYou: Worth a note for automated playtesting of the action RPG's combat and crafting loops, once results firm up.
